newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Export wins spread in system.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Export wins spread in system.

text.p: Attention turned to Australia's new wheat crop last week as payoffs from the current season's successful wheat export drive spread through the system.
Cash grain markets remained flat, leaving the main action to Australian Wheat Board (AWB) pool price increases for current wheat and estimates for new crop wheat.
The AWB's unexpected further boost to current wheat pool prices, by A$3.00 a tonne to A$198.00 for Australian Standard White (ASW), was the direct consequence of export wins.
It announced during the week it had produced a A$100 million bonus in export income from striking early export deals and calculated risk-taking on carryover stocks.
The AWB's increase in its estimate of 1997/98 pool prices, to A$175.00-A$185.00 a tonne from A$170.00-A$180.00, left room for further price increases, futures brokers said.

But the trade also saw an indirect message in the AWB's first tender sale of wheat from the national wheat pool this year. "It probably sends a message to the market that the AWB is prepared to sell and will set some sort of ceiling (on prices)," said one trader, who asked not to be named.
AWB announced during the week it had sold 5,000 tonnes of ASW at A$193.00 a tonne delivered Geelong, breaking a string of five "no deal" tenders.

Sydney Futures Exchange wheat reacted to the increased 1997/98 pool estimate with rising prices in more distant contracts. Over the week the recently-active January 1998 contract rose to A$172.00 from A$169.00 a tonne.

Australian wheat shipments slackened off slightly last week but remained at a high level, with 268,414 tonnes moved. This brought exports so far this shipping year, which begins October 1, to 10.54 million tonnes, up on 7.19 million tonnes last year.
Private crop forecasters hedged on whether Australia's new wheat crop was likely to be bigger than officially forecast.
Brian Bailey, principal of private forecast group Australian Wheat Forecasters, told Reuters on Friday his estimate of the 1997/98 wheat crop was about 17.80 million tonnes.

This is in line with the official forecast of 17.82 million tonnes by the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics but less than the approximately 19.0 million tonnes which Guy Allen of leading New South Wales (NSW) handling and storage group GrainCorp sees.
The crop was barely in the ground anywhere yet, leaving the argument to area sown, Bailey said.

"There's not a great deal between 16.0 million and 20.0 million tonnes. All we can say is soil moisture conditions are favourable for the top third of NSW and all of Queensland, and all we need is ideal sowing conditions to put that crop in.
"That means a light rain or two, spread a couple of weeks apart some time in May," he said.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders, a unit of Geneva-based international wheat trader Romak, said that with a quiet domestic grains market, the focus on new crop wheat was accompanied by a search for market direction from Chicago.
In the past week, domestic cash wheat held steady at about A$175.00 a tonne Newcastle, while sorghum for May delivery was down A$1.00-A$2.00 to A$160.00-A$162.00 a tonne.
"All eyes are on Chicago at the moment," he said. With the U.S. crop coming out, the unresolved issue was whether weather would affect the crop.
At week's end, Australian futures brokers were looking for a slight decline or consolidation in the Australian market after Chicago's sharp fall.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
